anchor: Whatever stirs this mortal frame
note: Frame: the body. Mortal means subject to death.

anchor: All are but ministers of Love
note: Ministers: servants, those who carry out another’s will.

anchor: Live o’er again that happy hour
note: O’er: over. Poets shorten the word to fit the meter.

anchor: When midway on the mount I lay
note: Mount: a hill or small mountain, here the slope where the ruined tower stands.

anchor: Beside the ruin’d tower
note: Ruin’d: fallen into ruins, in broken pieces.

anchor: The moonshine stealing o’er the scene
note: Stealing: moving gently and almost unnoticed.

anchor: She lean’d against the armed man
note: Armed man: a stone statue of a knight in armor on a tomb.

anchor: Few sorrows hath she of her own
note: Hath: has. An old form used to give the poem a ballad flavor.

anchor: I play’d a soft and doleful air
note: Doleful: full of sorrow. Air: a tune.

anchor: I sang an old and moving story
note: Moving: stirring the feelings, touching.

anchor: An old rude song
note: Rude: simple and rough, not polished.

anchor: That ruin wild and hoary
note: Hoary: gray or white with age, very old.

anchor: ten long years he woo’d
note: Woo’d: courted, tried to win the love of.

anchor: I told her how he pined
note: Pined: wasted away with longing.

anchor: That crazed that bold and lovely Knight
note: Crazed: driven mad, deranged by his grief and rejection.

anchor: And sometimes from the darksome shade
note: Darksome: dark and gloomy, a shadowy place in the woods.

anchor: In green and sunny glade
note: Glade: an open space in a forest.

anchor: And that he knew it was a Fiend
note: Fiend: a devil or evil spirit.

anchor: And saved from outrage worse than death
note: Outrage: here, a violent assault. The phrase is a Victorian euphemism for rape.

anchor: And how she tended him in vain
note: Tended: nursed and looked after, as she cared for the sick knight.

anchor: And ever strove to expiate
note: Expiate: to make up for a wrong by suffering or doing good.

anchor: A dying man he lay
note: The knight is lying near death on the yellow leaves of autumn.

anchor: That tenderest strain of all the ditty
note: Strain: a stretch of music. Ditty: a short simple song.

anchor: Had thrill’d my guileless Genevieve
note: Guileless: honest, without any trickery.

anchor: The music and the doleful tale
note: Doleful: sad and mournful, full of grief.

anchor: The rich and balmy eve
note: Balmy: soft, mild, and soothing. Eve: evening.

anchor: And gentle wishes long subdued
note: Subdued: held back, kept down, as wishes she long hid.

anchor: Then suddenly, with timorous eye
note: Timorous: shy and fearful, easily frightened.

anchor: ’Twas partly love, and partly fear
note: ’Twas: it was, a contraction poets use to keep the meter.

anchor: And partly ’twas a bashful art
note: Bashful: shy and easily embarrassed.

anchor: My bright and beauteous Bride
note: Beauteous: beautiful, an old poetic form of the word.

anchor: Both were mine! Life went a-maying
note: Going a-Maying: in medieval and Tudor England, people rose at dawn on May Day and went to the woods for branches and flowers. Here it means youth spent in joy.

anchor: With Nature, Hope, and Poesy
note: Poesy: poetry, the art of writing verse.

anchor: This breathing house not built with hands
note: A biblical image: Paul calls the body an earthly house that will be dissolved, and the soul’s heavenly home a house “not made with hands.”
source: The Bible (King James Version), 2 Corinthians 5:1, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

anchor: This body that does me grievous wrong
note: Grievous: causing grief or pain. The old poet blames his aging body.

anchor: O’er aery cliffs and glittering sands
note: Aery: airy, high up, like an eagle’s nest.

anchor: Like those trim skiffs, unknown of yore
note: Skiffs: small light boats. Unknown of yore: not known in the past.

anchor: Nought cared this body for wind or weather
note: Nought: nothing. The body then cared nothing for weather.

anchor: Ere I was old?
note: Ere: before (an old word).

anchor: I’ll think it but a fond conceit
note: Conceit: a fanciful notion, an idle idea.

anchor: Thy vesper-bell hath not yet toll’d
note: Vesper-bell: the bell that calls people to evening prayer.

anchor: And thou wert aye a masker bold
note: Aye: always. Masker: one who wears a disguise.

anchor: What strange disguise hast now put on
note: Hast: have. The poet asks Youth what disguise he now wears.

anchor: I see these locks in silvery slips
note: Locks: hair. Slips: thin strands or locks.

anchor: Life is but Thought
note: A line of idealist philosophy: if life is only thought, then he can keep youth by thinking young.

anchor: With oft and tedious taking-leave
note: Oft: often. Tedious: tiresome, long and wearisome.

anchor: Like some poor nigh-related guest
note: Nigh-related: closely related, a near relative.
